raw_case_text: Our patient was a 65-year-old man who had ultra-low anterior resection and chemo-radiotherapy for rectal cancer. On follow-up computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis a year later, he was found to have a bladder mass (Fig. 1). He subsequently underwent elective TURBT and received intravesical mitomycin C (40 mg diluted in 40 ml of saline 0.9%) within 6 h post-operatively. Histology revealed non-invasive, low-grade TCC. Three weeks later, a follow-up CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was performed for routine follow-up of the rectal cancer; this scan incidentally detected calcification of the bladder wall at the surgical resection site (Fig. 1). He was asymptomatic. Cystoscopy and cystolitholapaxy was then performed for presumed bladder calculi, approximately three months after the TURBT. Extensive stone-like, whitish calcification of the bladder wall at the surgical resection site was found (Fig. 2), not merely slough or soft tissue material. These lesions were further resected down to the detrusor muscle layer as the material was not amenable to washout. Histology (Fig. 3) revealed chronic inflammation of urothelium and fragments of refractile, hard-edged material which was found to be made up of calcium phosphate. There were no features of malignancy. He had normal serum calcium and phosphate levels and no known history of exposure to tuberculosis or schistosomiasis or travel to Africa, Middle East or South East Asia. He had no symptoms of interstitial cystitis. Aside from the history of rectal cancer and associated therapy, he had no other relevant oncological history. He received intravenous fluorouracil, folinic acid and oxaliplatin adjuvant chemotherapy for rectal cancer with the final cycle administered more than 12 months prior to this diagnosis of bladder wall calcification. He never received any intravesical therapy prior to the single dose of mitomycin C administered after the initial TURBT. In view of the rapid onset and localized involvement of the resection site, the bladder wall calcification was most likely secondary to intravesical mitomycin C treatment. Since this episode, there was no further recurrence or long-term consequence. Thus, no further treatment was required aside from routine cystoscopy for follow-up of non-muscle invasive, low-grade bladder cancer.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old asymptomatic man was found to have an incidental bladder mass and subsequent resection-site calcification on surveillance CT 1 year after anterior resection and chemoradiotherapy for rectal cancer.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One year after ultra-low anterior resection and adjuvant chemoradiotherapy for rectal cancer, routine surveillance abdominal/pelvic CT detected an asymptomatic bladder mass. He underwent elective transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) followed within 6 hours by a single intravesical instillation of mitomycin C (40 mg in 40 mL 0.9% saline) for low-grade non-invasive transitional cell carcinoma (TCC). Three weeks post-TURBT, routine rectal cancer follow-up CT incidentally identified calcification at the bladder resection site while the patient remained completely asymptomatic.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of rectal cancer treated >12 months earlier with ultra-low anterior resection, chemoradiotherapy, and adjuvant IV 5-fluorouracil, folinic acid, and oxaliplatin. No prior intravesical therapy before the single post-TURBT mitomycin C dose; no history of exposure to tuberculosis or schistosomiasis; no travel to Africa, the Middle East, or Southeast Asia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Asymptomatic; denied symptoms of interstitial cystitis or lower urinary tract complaints.

objective.routine_investigations: Serum calcium and phosphate levels were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial surveillance abdominal/pelvic CT showed a bladder mass; initial TURBT histopathology confirmed non-invasive, low-grade urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma. Follow-up abdominal/pelvic CT 3 weeks post-TURBT showed focal calcification of the bladder wall at the resection site. Cystoscopy and cystolitholapaxy 3 months post-TURBT revealed extensive stone-like whitish calcifications adherent to the surgical resection site that required resection down to the detrusor muscle; repeat histopathology demonstrated chronic urothelial inflammation and refractile calcium phosphate deposits without residual malignancy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with localized dystrophic bladder wall calcification (encrusted cystitis) secondary to a single postoperative intravesical mitomycin C instillation following TURBT for non-muscle-invasive low-grade bladder cancer (with tuberculosis and schistosomiasis excluded by history and histology). Following transurethral resection of the calcified plaques down to the detrusor layer, he remained recurrence-free without long-term sequelae on routine surveillance cystoscopy.
